articles.title: Caregiver creep: how helping elderly relatives can snowball into a full-time job
articles.summary: Assisting an ageing loved one can start with small tasks but may lead to full-time caregiving that requires more support. Helping an ageing parent or loved one often begins with easy-to-field requests: Pick up a prescription. Drive them to a doctor’s appointment. Grab groceries.
body: However, light tasks – just “helping out” here and there – may eventually snowball into the avalanche of full-time caregiving, a phenomenon becoming known as “caregiver creep”. Like “ caregiver burnout ”, it’s not a formal term, but there is growing awareness about this slow build among healthcare providers and experts.

A 2025 research report from the AARP and the National Alliance for Caregiving found that 63 million Americans act as caregivers; one in every four adults is a caregiver and the majority (94%) are caring for an adult. As the population ages – the oldest baby boomers will turn 80 this year – the need for care will increase.

The US Bureau of Labor Statistics reports the majority (59%) of those providing this unpaid care are women. Many gen X and millennial women are feeling the sandwich-generation squeeze of caring for parents and children on top of their careers.

Recognizing when responsibilities increase, how to identify when support needs to level up, and where to find resources both for the person receiving care and the caregiver can help manage caregiver creep.

articles.title: A job that changed me: Being a theatre usher cracked open my heart to beauty
articles.summary: The performances often gave me goose bumps, but I also got to observe the highs and lows of audience behaviour. I was 24, had just moved into a share house I couldn’t afford, and my job as a nanny was proving less than ideal.
body: A friend had told me to apply to become a front-of-house staff member at Australia’s busiest performing arts centre, Arts Centre Melbourne. It was a rare opportunity, as people rarely quit. To be surrounded by art again sounded like a dream.

I progressed to the final interview round. Anxious about nailing it and unable to study for it – for some unknown reason, a maths quiz was involved – I focused purely on appearance. I blew my budget on a blow wave, planning to charm the interviewers with my perfect hair and Target office-casual best.
Whether it was my hair or the secret texts to my friend asking for help answering the maths quiz, I got the job.

articles.title: Met Gala exhibition honoring John Galliano is cancelled after backlash
articles.summary: Fashion designer was convicted of hate crime by French court in 2011 after series of racist and antisemitic remarks. The controversial fashion designer John Galliano announced on Monday that an exhibition honoring his work that New York’s Metropolitan Museum of Art had scheduled to open for the…
body: The museum’s decision to honor Galliano, who was convicted of a hate crime by a French court in 2011 after a series of racist and antisemitic remarks, had drawn controversy and backlash.

“After much reflection and discussion with all those involved, I have decided, with great sadness, that it is best for the exhibition not to take place at this time,” Galliano wrote in a statement posted on Instagram on Monday morning.
The exhibition, titled John Galliano: Horizons, was announced in early August and was set to have been kicked off by the annual Met Gala.

In his statement on Monday saying that the exhibition was off, Galliano wrote: “I remain fully accountable for the pain caused by my words in the past, particularly the hurt I caused to the Jewish and Asian communities, and I remain deeply sorry.

articles.title: The 99 Most Memorable Venice Film Festival Looks of All Time
articles.summary: Known as one of the most glamorous film festivals in the world, you can always count on spellbinding style in Venice. See the best celebrity looks here over the years.
body: Red carpet followers, you will be pleased to know: The 2026 Venice Film Festival is officially here this week.

Running from September 2 to September 12, the glitzy ceremony—known as one of the most glamorous film events in the world—is set to deliver a stellar red carpet filled with A-listers. And with expected stars like Amal and George Clooney, Penélope Cruz, and Maggie Gyllenhaal on the roster this year, you can certainly count on a splashy array of custom gowns.

The Venice Film Festival has a history of delivering memorable red carpet moments, after all. Since its inception in 1932, the Italian festival has long seen top Hollywood stars descend upon the affair (in their gondolas, of course) wearing their finest formal attire. Compared to the rigid red carpet rules that come with, say, Cannes, Venice is more free-spirited and fun—meaning, you can always count on the actors in attendance to take risks and truly go for it.

articles.title: Why You Might Need to Roll Back Windows' Latest Update
articles.summary: If you're the kind of person who installs Windows updates as soon as they hit your PC, you're likely running version KB5120998 of Windows 11 right now. Microsoft released it on Thursday, and while it's an optional update, it isn't locked behind its Windows Insider program.
body: As reported by Windows Insider, the latest Windows 11 update is a big one. It includes some major updates to Windows customization, including changes that Microsoft has been testing for months. For example, the update lets you move and resize the taskbar however you like, and there are other changes that improve Windows Search for the better. These updates have previouly been exclusive to Insiders, but are now officially part of Windows 11. But it's not all good news.

In addition to these new features, it seems Microsoft inadvertently shipped some bugs with this update. Perhaps the most impactful of them, and the one most users will notice right away, is an issue where the cursor doesn't appear onscreen—or, when it does, it appears too big or too small. Some users report their cursors are enormous, while others find them annoyingly small. Unless you use your keyboard to control everything on your PC, losing access to your cursor isn't really an option, and even inconsistent UI experiences aren't really acceptable in 2026, considering Windows has had a cursor since 1985.

articles.title: “It’s Optimism for Futurism”: Ambush’s Yoon Ahn Gives Barbie Her Own Humanoid Twist
articles.summary: Prototype 001 isn’t like other Barbies—she’s a robo-babe with a blonde hime haircut, a pink headset, silver body armor, and a cyborg cat companion.
body: The ensemble draws inspiration via an assortment of sources, including the character uniforms from anime TV shows and sci-fi movies as well as her favorite contemporary artist, Mariko Mori. “Her work often explores the themes of technology, spirituality, and transcendence,” explains Ahn. “It was also kind of my headspace of, What does it mean to be human and humanoid at the same time? This is where we’re going with everything. In the history of Mattel, it’s probably the first humanoid Barbie.”

articles.title: Inside the French Riviera Holiday Home of the Late Fashion Icon Jacqueline de Ribes
articles.summary: The fashion designer and style icon Jacqueline de Ribes, who died in 2025, spent her summers at this home high above the Gulf of Saint-Tropez—here, her granddaughter Alix de La Rochefoucauld allows Vogue a look inside.
body: Although fashion designer and style icon Jacqueline de Ribes loved the light at Les Hauts de Saint Marc, her Provençal house sitting high above the Gulf of Saint-Tropez, she rarely saw the morning there. Preferring to linger long past noon in her 18th-century mahogany Portuguese bed, nibbling dry toast and sipping tea in a negligee, she would emerge around teatime or just before dinner.

Holding court in caftans cinched with a jeweled belt, sometimes slit to the hip well into her 70s, she always arrived last and was unquestionably the most glamorous person in the room. Even 50 years into their marriage, her granddaughter Alix de La Rochefoucauld recalls that her grandfather, Count Edouard de Ribes, still watched his wife arrive “with stars in his eyes.”
